item.title: The courtesy of phenomenology — Wed Aug 26, 3:00 PM — Jackman Humanities Building
item.description: Speaker: Jocelyn Benoist, University of Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne Phenomenology starts from a presupposition: that it is meaningful to treat everything as “appearing.” This postulate is, of course, linked to the Western metaphysics of subjectivity, of which phenomenology is the ultimate product—even if phenomenologists claim regularly to overcome it. This unconditional application of the notion of “appearing” raises a grammatical problem, for the verb “to appear” seems to have quite specific conditions of use that are incompatible with any absolutization. A self-sufficiency of appearing is just inconceivable. In other words, there are ontological conditions to phenomenology. Highlighting these, however, will only be the first step of my analysis. item.title: The Board and the Empire: Satyajit Ray’s Shatranj Ke Khilari — Sat Sep 5, 2:00 PM — Aga Khan Museum
item.description:
Presented in conjunction with Game On! and programmed by film scholar, author, critic, and curator Narendra Pachkhédé, this screening of Satyajit Ray’s Shatranj Ke Khilari ( The Chess Players ) explores chess as a cultural form and a lens on power, strategy, and political inaction.
A brief introduction by Pachkédé will connect the film to three works in the exhibition. A 12th-century Iranian chess set, the Shahnameh folio “Buzurjmihr Masters the Indian Game of Chess,” and Yoko Ono’s Play It By Trust . Together, they trace chess from its material and courtly histories to its modern role as a space of cooperation.
The screening will be followed by a conversation between Bita Pourvash, curator of Game On! , and Narendra Pachkhédé, film scholar, author, critic, and curator, exploring what games reveal about conflict, responsibility, and historical change.
Source: Aga Khan Museum
